clue.text: "Like the red rose of summer that blooms in the day / - slowly and fades away" (Bob Dylan)

definitions.text: "Like the red rose of summer that blooms in the day / - slowly and fades away" (Bob Dylan)

parts.words: "Like the red rose of summer that blooms in the day / - slowly and fades away" (Bob Dylan)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing words open the second line of a Dylan song from the album New Morning

explanation.surface: A lyric about a summer rose with the opening words of its second line left out.
explanation.walkthrough: No wordplay here: the solver supplies the gap in the quoted Dylan lyric from knowledge of the song.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's title phrase completes the line, saying the hours drag by slowly.

clue.text: Police upset taking initially horrific Wendall family account

indicators.note: taking means the police word holds the next letter inside it
in a down clue, upset means the word for police is turned upside down, read bottom to top

parts.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police

indicators.note: initially means only the opening letter of horrific is used

explanation.surface: Disturbed police take on a horrific story about one family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns MET into TEM, and 'taking' puts H inside it after the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce Carol Oates's novel follows the Wendall family of Detroit, so it is their story in book form.

clue.text: Coat and headwear that you must put on for Ars Nova figure

parts.note: a mac is a raincoat, short for mackintosh

indicators.note: the headwear must take on the letter for you, which goes inside it

parts.note: a hat is headwear
U is text-speak for you

explanation.surface: Instructions to don a coat and a hat before playing a medieval musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must put on' tells you the letter for 'you' goes inside the headwear. 'Ars Nova' is the French musical style of the 1300s.
explanation.definitionFit: Guillaume de Machaut was the leading French composer and poet of the fourteenth-century Ars Nova style.

clue.text: Country Life writer awfully deprecatory, king admitted

indicators.note: admitted means the king's letter is let in among the others
awfully suggests the word deprecatory is mangled, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A disparaging writer for a country magazine has let in royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awfully' shuffles DEPRECATORY and 'admitted' slips K in among those letters. Country Life is also a well-known British magazine about rural living, which is the surface trap.
explanation.definitionFit: Ackroyd's first poetry collection, published in 1978, was titled Country Life, making him its author.

clue.text: Novel about a neurosurgeon writing article on Pooh in Express

indicators.note: in means the article and the pooh word sit inside the word for express

parts.note: to express something is to say it

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it, so the article comes first

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
pooh is slang for excrement, a turd

explanation.surface: A fast train carries a book whose author writes rudely about a bear named Pooh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts the article first in a down entry, and 'in' tucks both inside the word for express. Pooh looks like Winnie-the-Pooh and Express like a newspaper or train; both are decoys.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian McEwan's 2005 book follows one day in the life of the brain surgeon Henry Perowne.

clue.text: Piece of music in blue books foremost of tenors ignored

indicators.note: ignored means that letter is left out of the word for blue books

parts.note: blue means smutty, so blue books are erotica

indicators.note: foremost of means the leading letter of tenors is taken

explanation.surface: Somewhere in a stack of racy books, a passage about tenors is skipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignored' removes the T (the first letter of 'tenors', from 'foremost of') from EROTICA.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's Third Symphony carries this name, the Italian for heroic.

clue.text: Lady Hermione's hair accessory or Oscar's brother

parts.note: Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet
brother as a friendly address means pal

explanation.surface: A guess at whether a lady's hairpiece or Oscar Wilde's sibling is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scott's Anne of Geierstein, the Baroness Hermione wears in her hair a gem that changes colour with her moods. 'Oscar' suggests Wilde; it is a phonetic-alphabet letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The stone Scott's Hermione wore in her hair is the iridescent gem, worn there as an ornament.

clue.text: Moral lesson in paperback about vagrant

indicators.note: about means the paperback letters go around the vagrant

parts.note: PB is the usual abbreviation for paperback
a rover is a wanderer, a vagrant

explanation.surface: A paperback tells a moralising tale about a tramp.
explanation.definitionFit: A short saying that states a moral truth, as in the biblical book of sayings.

clue.text: New retailer stocking Trade Union books?

indicators.note: stocking means the rearranged letters hold the union abbreviation, as a shop holds goods
New means the letters of retailer are made over in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A new shop stocking books about trade unions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges the letters of 'retailer' into LITERARE, and 'stocking' puts the union abbreviation into the middle of that.
explanation.definitionFit: Written works taken together, especially those valued as art, are what a bookshop shelves.

clue.text: Sensation produced by previous quotation

parts.note: ex as a prefix means former or previous
a citation is a quotation from a source

explanation.surface: An earlier quotation causes a stir.
explanation.definitionFit: Excitement or a thrill of feeling, as when a nerve is stimulated.

clue.text: One supplying lines and ecstasy-laced marijuana

indicators.note: laced means the drug is mixed into the marijuana, so it goes inside

parts.note: pot is slang for marijuana
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A dealer supplying lines of cocaine and spiked cannabis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lines' suggests cocaine in a drug surface; here it means lines of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of verse provides the lines that make up a poem.

clue.text: One who backed a president who wrote feminist works

parts.note: an angel is a financial backer, especially of a theatre show
Jimmy Carter was a US president

explanation.surface: A political donor who supported a president and also wrote feminist books.
explanation.definitionFit: The English author of The Bloody Chamber reworked fairy tales from a strongly feminist angle.

clue.text: He put down Jennie Baxter and Rod on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio means a word is heard rather than seen, so its sound is what counts

parts.note: a bar is a rod of metal or wood

explanation.surface: A man killed off someone called Jennie Baxter, and a man named Rod broadcast it.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Barr wrote the novel Jennie Baxter, Journalist (1899). 'put down' suggests killing; here it means writing down.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish-Canadian novelist committed this heroine to paper, writing her story.

clue.text: Yarn delivery agent near court taking a new order

indicators.note: taking a new order says the letters of near and court are rearranged

explanation.surface: A courier from the wool trade, near a court, is reorganised.
explanation.walkthrough: Yarn suggests wool and delivery agent a courier; really they are a story and its telling.
explanation.definitionFit: A skilled storyteller delivers tales, or yarns, to listeners.

clue.text: Cossack and sailor lamp a grasping Anglo-Saxon

indicators.note: grasping means the sailor, lamp and a together hold the Anglo-Saxon abbreviation

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor
a bulb is the lamp in a light fitting

explanation.surface: A Cossack and a sailor fight over a lamp held by an Anglo-Saxon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grasping' sets the Anglo-Saxon abbreviation just after the sailor. Taras Bulba is Gogol's 1835 novella.
explanation.definitionFit: Gogol's novella is named after its hero, an old Zaporozhian Cossack commander.

clue.text: Coffee loving, perhaps observed by Yard in Huxley work

parts.note: someone who loves coffee might be against tea: anti, against, plus cha, slang for tea

explanation.surface: A coffee addict observed by Scotland Yard in a book by Huxley.
explanation.walkthrough: Cha (char) is British slang for tea, so preferring coffee makes one 'anti-cha'.
explanation.definitionFit: Aldous Huxley's 1923 satirical novel of London bohemians bears this title.

clue.text: It was one of her characters Bishop found in Stein novel

definitions.text: It was one of her characters

indicators.note: found in means the bishop letter is placed inside the rearranged letters
novel as an adjective means new, signalling a fresh arrangement of stein

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop turns up in a novel by Gertrude Stein.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' shuffles STEIN to NESIT and 'found in' puts B inside. 'It' is the sand-fairy of Five Children and It.
explanation.definitionFit: Edith, the children's author, created the wish-granting sand-fairy known as It.

clue.text: He co-engineered a "Difference Engine" using British money

definitions.meaning: Bruce of that surname co-wrote the steampunk novel The Difference Engine with William Gibson
the pound is the British currency, also called by this name

explanation.surface: An engineer built a calculating machine with British funding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'co-engineered' suggests Babbage's machine; it means co-wrote the novel of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Pound sterling is the official name of the UK currency; Bruce is the American science-fiction author.

clue.text: When police announced where spirits were found?

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

indicators.note: announced means the police word is spoken, so its sound gives the letters

parts.note: a guard is a police officer in Ireland, a member of the Garda

explanation.surface: A question about where police said spirits turned up, perhaps in a raid.
explanation.walkthrough: Spirits suggests drink or ghosts; it means the Norse gods.
explanation.definitionFit: In Norse myth this is the home of the gods, the divine beings who live there.

clue.text: Needing a break, Granddad and I planned Father's Day

parts.note: a grand is slang for a thousand pounds, abbreviated G
a dad is an old man, informally a father

explanation.surface: Grandad and I organised a celebration for fathers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needing a break' tells you to split 'Granddad' into 'grand' (G) and 'dad' (OLD MAN). William Goldman wrote the novel Father's Day (1971).
explanation.definitionFit: The American novelist and screenwriter wrote Father's Day, so he speaks as its planner.

clue.text: What Meursault might be called by some is more foreign

definitions.text: What Meursault might be called by some
definitions.meaning: Camus's novel about Meursault is translated in some editions under this English title rather than The Outsider
the comparative of an adjective for unfamiliar or alien

explanation.surface: Camus's hero is labelled by some as more alien than the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Camus's L'Étranger appears in American translation under this title; the comparative means odder or more unfamiliar.

clue.text: All kegs must be changed for Brontë biographer

indicators.note: must be changed says the letters of all and kegs are rearranged

explanation.surface: Every barrel has to be swapped for a writer about the Brontës.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth, the Victorian novelist, wrote the 1857 Life of Charlotte Brontë.

clue.text: Book by Rankin, possibly, about a jealous lover

parts.note: Ian Rankin is the crime writer, so his forename is the example
ca, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: A Rankin crime novel about a jealous lover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rankin, possibly' points to Ian Rankin, the Scottish crime writer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Othello, Cassio's mistress flares with jealousy over the handkerchief he gives her.

clue.text: Fanciful type in American club by revolving bar

parts.note: a billy club is an American police truncheon

indicators.note: revolving means the word for bar is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: a rail is a bar

explanation.surface: A fantasist in an American nightclub next to a rotating bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolving' turns RAIL into LIAR. Club suggests a nightclub; it is a truncheon.
explanation.definitionFit: Keith Waterhouse's daydreaming hero of the 1959 novel lives in fantasies, a habitual fibber.

clue.text: A bachelor meeting European son that's turned 10?

indicators.note: that's turned means the European and son letters are read backwards

explanation.surface: A single man meets a European son who has just reached ten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's turned' reverses E and S into SE. '10' points to the answer of 10 Across, a writer of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Dannie, the Welsh writer and doctor, was a noted poet, as 10 Across asks.

clue.text: Perhaps a revolutionary place where Wooster went

indicators.note: revolutionary means turning round, so the word for perhaps a goes backwards

parts.note: A is an example of a musical note

explanation.surface: A school that may have bred revolutionaries, where Wooster studied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' turns NOTE around. Bertie Wooster, Wodehouse's hero, went to the famous English public school.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertie Wooster is an Old Etonian, having been educated at the Windsor school.

clue.text: Maiden in labour is one producing Shakespearean tales

indicators.note: in means the maiden letter goes inside the labour word

parts.note: Lab is the abbreviation for the Labour Party
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A young woman in labour gives birth to stories.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden in cricket is an over with no runs scored. 'labour' suggests childbirth; it is the political party.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles and his sister Mary wrote Tales from Shakespeare (1807), retelling the plays for children.

clue.text: "The Jury had each formed a different view / (Long before the — was read), / And they all spoke at once, so that none of them knew / One word that the others had said" (Lewis Carroll)

definitions.text: "The Jury had each formed a different view / (Long before the — was read), / And they all spoke at once, so that none of them knew / One word that the others had said" (Lewis Carroll)

parts.words: "The Jury had each formed a different view / (Long before the — was read), / And they all spoke at once, so that none of them knew / One word that the others had said" (Lewis Carroll)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from The Hunting of the Snark, Fit the Sixth, the Barrister's Dream of a trial

explanation.surface: Carroll's jury reaching its verdict before the charge is read.
explanation.walkthrough: No wordplay: the gap is filled from knowledge of Carroll's poem.
explanation.definitionFit: The formal charge read out in court before a trial is what the jurors had prejudged.

clue.text: To Eyre, Reed was one emaciated in looks without any good at all

indicators.note: without any means the letter for good is dropped entirely

parts.note: gaunt means looking haggard and emaciated

explanation.surface: Mrs Reed looked thin and had no goodness in her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without any' removes G from GAUNT. Mrs Reed is the cruel relative who brings up the orphan Jane in Jane Eyre.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Reed is Jane's maternal relative by marriage, her uncle's widow.

clue.text: Lover of Homer near London arresting a right bastard?

indicators.note: arresting means the first pieces catch and hold a and right inside them

parts.note: Marge is Homer Simpson's wife in The Simpsons

explanation.surface: A lover of the poet Homer near London apprehends a real scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: Homer suggests the Greek poet, which suits a Trojan answer; it is Homer Simpson. In Troilus and Cressida, Margarelon is a bastard son of Priam.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare names him as Priam's illegitimate son, one born out of wedlock.
